tools.name: EnterWorktree
tools.description:
Use this tool ONLY when explicitly instructed to work in a worktree — either by the user directly, or by project instructions (CLAUDE.md / memory). This tool creates an isolated git worktree and switches the current session into it.

## When to Use

- The user explicitly says "worktree" (e.g., "start a worktree", "work in a worktree", "create a worktree", "use a worktree")
- CLAUDE.md or memory instructions direct you to work in a worktree for the current task

## When NOT to Use

- The user asks to create a branch, switch branches, or work on a different branch — use git commands instead
- The user asks to fix a bug or work on a feature — use normal git workflow unless worktrees are explicitly requested by the user or project instructions
- Never use this tool unless "worktree" is explicitly mentioned by the user or in CLAUDE.md / memory instructions

## Requirements

- Must be in a git repository, OR have WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks configured in settings.json
- Must not already be in a worktree session when creating a new worktree (`name`); switching into another existing worktree via `path` is allowed

## Behavior

- In a git repository: creates a new git worktree inside `.claude/worktrees/` on a new branch. The base ref is governed by the `worktree.baseRef` setting: `fresh` (default) branches from origin/<default-branch>; `head` branches from your current local HEAD
- Outside a git repository: delegates to WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks for VCS-agnostic isolation
- Switches the session's working directory to the new worktree
- Use ExitWorktree to leave the worktree mid-session (keep or remove). On session exit, if still in the worktree, the user will be prompted to keep or remove it

## Entering an existing worktree

Pass `path` instead of `name` to switch the session into a worktree that already exists (e.g., one you just created with `git worktree add`). On first entry from the launch directory, the path must appear in `git worktree list` for the repository that owns it — the current repository or, in a multi-repo workspace, a repository nested inside it; paths registered by neither are rejected. ExitWorktree will not remove a worktree entered this way; use `action: "keep"` to return to the original directory.

Switching with `path` also works when the session is already in a worktree (the previous worktree is left on disk, untouched, and only the new one is tracked for exit-time cleanup), and from agents whose working directory was pinned at launch (subagent isolation or explicit cwd). In both cases the target must be a worktree under `.claude/worktrees/` of the same repository, and from a pinned agent the switch only affects this agent, not the parent session. After a further switch, previously-visited worktrees are no longer writable — re-issue EnterWorktree with `path` to return to one.

## Parameters

- `name` (optional): A name for a new worktree. If neither `name` nor `path` is provided, a random name is generated.
- `path` (optional): Path to an existing worktree to enter instead of creating one — of the current repository, or (on first entry from the launch directory) of a repository nested inside it. Mutually exclusive with `name`.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/claude-stack-doctor

# Claude Stack Doctor

One command surfaces every known silent-failure class in the automation/memory stack. Run it before debugging anything by hand.

## Quick start

```bash
/opt/homebrew/bin/pwsh -NoProfile -File ~/.claude/skills/claude-stack-doctor/scripts/stack-check.ps1
```

Exit 0 = all clear. Exit 1 = the VERDICT line lists issue codes. Report the findings to the user, then apply the matching fix below.

## Cross-machine handoff (runs on BOTH machines)

`scripts/handoff-check.ps1` is the one part of this skill that is not Mac-only, and it can be run on its own:

```
powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $HOME\.claude\skills\claude-stack-doctor\scripts\handoff-check.ps1
```

It answers a question nothing else here asked: did state actually make the trip between the two machines? Every other check verifies a component. This verifies the path.

The failure it exists to catch: `daily-backup` pushes `global-memory` nightly and, until 2026-09-12, nothing on the receiving machine ever pulled it. The Windows laptop was found 4 commits behind with every other signal reading healthy, because the backup section measures `ahead` only — which catches a broken push and is blind to a missing pull.

Issue codes:

- `handoff-memory-stale` — `global-memory` is behind origin. This is the serious one: memory written on the other machine is on GitHub and not here, so this session is running on stale context. Fix with `/startup`, or `git -C ~/.claude/global-memory pull --no-rebase`.
- `handoff-behind:<repo>` — config, skills or notes behind origin. Same fix, lower stakes.
- `handoff-unpushed:<repo>` — this machine is more than 3 commits ahead. The other machine cannot see this work; run `/closeout`.
- `handoff-fetch:<repo>` — offline, or GitHub auth has rotted.
- `handoff-repo-gone:<repo>` — the folder is present but is not a git repo. Something replaced a synced repo with a plain folder and its contents are going nowhere.
- A repo absent from the machine entirely is skipped, not failed. `SecondBrain` is Mac-only and its absence on Windows is correct.

The "memory flow" line reports how long since `origin/main` on `global-memory` last advanced. Over 14 days it says so without failing: it cannot distinguish "quiet fortnight" from "the other machine's backup stopped pushing", and a check that cries wolf during the first gets ignored during the second.

**This machine is macOS** (migrated 2026-08-05). Jobs are **launchd user agents** in `~/Library/LaunchAgents/`, not Task Scheduler. The script is PowerShell only because `pwsh` runs it natively; it checks launchd. PowerShell on macOS normalises `\` inside a path string to `/`, so the script's mixed separators resolve correctly — verified 2026-08-29. Do not "fix" them.

Useful launchd commands:
```bash
launchctl list | grep keystone                                    # loaded jobs + last exit code
launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/com.keystone.<name>                  # live schedule and state
launchctl bootout  gui/$(id -u)/com.keystone.<name>               # unload
launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.keystone.<name>.plist   # reload
```
Edit a schedule with `/usr/libexec/PlistBuddy -c "Set :StartCalendarInterval:Hour <n>" <plist>`, then bootout + bootstrap. **A plist edit alone does nothing until it is reloaded.**

## Weekly scheduled run

launchd agent `com.keystone.stackdoctor` (Mondays 10:30) runs `scripts/weekly-check.ps1`: the same read-only check, unattended. On failure it appends a one-line summary to `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log` (surfaced at every session start per CLAUDE.md) and the full output is always in `scripts/last-weekly-run.log`. When a session surfaces such an entry, run this skill interactively to diagnose and fix, then clear the entry from `.errors.log`.

**Clearing `.errors.log`:** shell truncation (`: > file`) anywhere under `$HOME` is blocked by dcg rule `core.filesystem:redirect-truncate-root-home`. Use `cp /dev/null <file>`. There is no `truncate` binary on this machine. Archive first — the lines are often live issues, not stale history:
```bash
cp ~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log ~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log.archived-$(date +%Y-%m-%d)
cp /dev/null ~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log
```

## Known failure classes and fixes

These four classes have each bitten more than once (evidence: daily logs 2026-04 → 2026-07). Match the issue code to its fix:

### `task:*` / `task-stale:*` — launchd agent failed or didn't run
1. Read the `action:` line the script printed and run that exact command **manually in a foreground terminal** — launchd discards stdout unless the plist sets `StandardOutPath`; foreground shows the real error.
2. Known root causes: executable referenced without a full path (launchd agents get a minimal PATH — always use full paths like `/opt/homebrew/bin/pwsh`, and set `EnvironmentVariables:PATH` in the plist); a plist edited but never `bootout`+`bootstrap`ed, so the old schedule is still live; the job firing at an hour the required volume is unmounted (see `backup-*`).
3. `launchctl list | grep keystone` shows each job's **last exit code** in column 2. A non-zero there with no output means the script's own log is the only evidence — check `~/.claude/scripts/logs/` and for a `*.log` beside the script.

### `venv-missing` / `venv-broken` — Python venv rot
The script checks `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/.venv/bin/python`.
macOS root causes: a Homebrew `python3` major-version bump orphans venvs built against the old interpreter; a `uv` reinstall or relocation breaks tools that hardcode `/Users/kristinarash/.local/bin/uv` (CLAUDE.md forbids relocating it for this reason).
Fix: recreate the venv (`uv sync` in the project, or `python3 -m venv .venv` + reinstall from its pyproject), then run the dependent agent once by hand to confirm.
*History (Windows box, retired 2026-08-14): Python Install Manager migrations deleted `C:\Python31x` twice, silently killing morning-briefing for 6 days. The lesson transfers — an interpreter move breaks every venv built on it — the paths do not.*

### `memsearch-path` / `memsearch-run` — memsearch CLI broken
memsearch is a **uv tool** on this machine: binary at `/Users/kristinarash/.local/bin/memsearch`, environment at `/Users/kristinarash/.local/share/uv/tools/memsearch/`.
- Not on PATH or the binary errors → reinstall with `uv tool install --force memsearch`, not pip.
- Import failures inside the tool env (e.g. `onnxruntime`) are testable directly:
  `/Users/kristinarash/.local/share/uv/tools/memsearch/bin/python -c "import onnxruntime; print(onnxruntime.__version__)"`
- **After ANY reinstall/upgrade of memsearch the local flush patch is stripped.** Re-apply it (notes in `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/`), then confirm `.errors.log` stays empty for a session.
- `INDEX full set: Indexed 0 chunks` in the nightly log is **usually not an indexer fault** — it means nothing new arrived. Check `flush-stale` first; a dead flush pipeline starves the indexer and looks identical (confirmed 2026-08-29).

### `errors-log` / `flush-stale` / `flush-error` / `flush-missing` — memory pipeline
- `.errors.log` non-empty → read the entries **before clearing**; they are frequently live unresolved issues rather than stale history. Common causes: the stripped memsearch flush patch (above), or an Agent SDK timeout ("Control request timeout: initialize" — transient, but recurring daily means the hook environment is broken).
- `last-flush.json` stale >48h → check `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/scripts/flush.log` tail for the real error. `last-flush.json` is written by `flush.py` **only on success**, so a stale timestamp means flushes are dying, not that the hook never fired.
- **Stranded context files are the tell.** `session-end.py` writes `scripts/session-flush-<session>-<stamp>.md` then spawns `flush.py`, which **deletes that file on success**. So every leftover `session-flush-*.md` in `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/scripts/` is a flush that died, and its date maps to a missing `daily/<date>.md`.
  Recover one by re-running it by hand (~1 min, writes into the daily log):
  ```bash
  /Users/kristinarash/.local/bin/uv run --directory ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler \
    python ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/scripts/flush.py <context-file> <session-id>
  ```
  Success looks like `Result: FLUSH_OK` + `Flush complete` in `flush.log`.
- No `SessionEnd fired` lines in `flush.log` for days, yet the hook works when run by hand → sessions are being closed rather than exited cleanly. Self-verifying: end one session normally and re-check the tail.
- FLUSH_ERROR in dailies → same investigation; `flush.log` is ground truth.

### `backup-*` — daily backup rot
launchd agent `com.keystone.dailybackup` (**09:00 daily** since 2026-08-29) runs `~/.claude/scripts/daily-backup.ps1`: auto-commits+pushes the memory repos (SecondBrain, dotclaude, claude-skills, claude-global-memory), **rsync**-snapshots `~/.claude/projects`, `~/.codex`, `~/.gemini` and non-repo DEV folders to Google Drive at `~/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-eric.rash11@gmail.com/My Drive/…`, captures the same set to the **CRASHBOX SSD** at `/Volumes/CRASHBOX/AssistantBackup/` when it is mounted, runs an uncapped full memsearch reindex, and resets the hook's timeout-streak counter. Restore procedure: `~/.claude/RESTORE.md`.

**The SSD layer's signature failure — a clean exit code is not evidence.** If CRASHBOX is unmounted the run logs `TARGET SSD … NOT MOUNTED … SKIPPED` and still ends `OK (0 errors)`. The schedule moved 00:30 → 09:00 on 2026-08-29 precisely because the drive was never attached at 00:30. **Verify an SSD capture only by a fresh receipt** at `/Volumes/CRASHBOX/AssistantBackup/_receipts/run-*.txt`. Never by directory mtimes (`rsync -a` preserves source mtimes, and a parent dir's mtime moves only when an entry is added or removed — top-level SSD dirs legitimately show weeks-old dates after a perfect capture) and never by `du`. `-DryRun` runs `rsync -n` and proves nothing about writes.
- `backup-missing` / `backup-stale` → job didn't run; re-run foreground (~6 min): `/opt/homebrew/bin/pwsh -File ~/.claude/scripts/daily-backup.ps1`. There is no SSD-only switch, and one should not be added.
- `backup-error` → read `~/.claude/scripts/logs/daily-backup.log`; a `repo-diverged:*` entry means a memory repo has both remote and local changes — reconcile manually (the script refuses to merge from automation).
- `backup-repo-drift:*` → pushes failing (>3 unpushed commits); usually gh/git auth rot — run `gh auth status`.
- `backup-cloud-*` → the Drive-API heartbeat (gws CLI queries RESTORE.md's cloud modifiedTime). `-check` = gws auth rot; re-auth needs explicit full scope URLs: `gws auth login --scopes "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/calendar.readonly"` (the `-s drive` shorthand silently grants NO scopes, v0.22.5 bug). After re-auth delete `~/.config/gws/token_cache.json` or it serves the stale token. The login is interactive — Eric must run it himself via `!` while at the machine, then open the printed URL directly; terminal copy/paste truncates it at line-wrap. `-stale`/`-missing` = files reach the local CloudStorage cache but Google Drive for Desktop isn't syncing — check that Google Drive is running and signed in.
- Drive is a **FUSE CloudStorage mount**: it rounds mtimes it did not write, so `rsync -a` re-sends identical files forever. Use `--modify-window=5`; never `--size-only`.

## Not covered by the script (check manually if symptoms point there)

- **MCP/plugin auth rot** (9 manual fix-it sessions on record): run `claude doctor` / `claude mcp list` and re-auth any claude.ai connectors showing failures (Supabase, Vercel, Google Calendar have all rotted before).
- **Catapult OpenField token expiry**: see the auth section of `pp-catapult-openfield-connect`.

## Rules

- Read-only by default: the script never mutates state. Fixes are applied by you, deliberately, after reporting findings.
- Don't assume the obvious culprit — a signal that pattern-matches a known failure may have a different cause (lesson: 6/25 Milvus/ETIMEDOUT misdiagnosis). Confirm with the foreground re-run before fixing.
- When a fix is applied, re-run the script to verify the issue code clears, and note the incident in memory if it's a new failure class.

content.content: Launching skill: dev-sync

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/dev-sync

# DEV sync

Eric works on a Mac and a Windows laptop. GitHub (`erash11`, all private) is the transport. This skill makes the current machine match GitHub without losing anything on either side. It is the first thing to run when sitting down at a machine.

## Step 0: find DEV (never depend on cwd)

Eric may run this from anywhere. Detect the machine and go to its DEV root:

- macOS (`uname` = Darwin): `~/DEV`
- Windows (PowerShell, or `$OS` = Windows_NT): `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV`

If that folder does not exist, stop and say so. Do not guess another location. Print the root you chose on the first line of output.

## Step 1: config and skills

These are separate repos and the other machine may have changed them:

1. `~/.claude` (repo `dotclaude`): `git pull`. If `~/.claude/machine.md` is missing, copy `machine.macos.md` or `machine.windows.md` to `machine.md` for this OS.
2. `~/.claude/skills` (repo `claude-skills`): `git pull`, then run `sync-to-codex.sh` (Mac) or `sync-to-codex.ps1` (Windows) so Codex sees the shared skills.
3. `~/.claude/global-memory` (repo `claude-global-memory`): `git pull`. **This is the only thing that carries memory between the two machines.** USER.md, MEMORY.md and the handoffs live here. `daily-backup` pushes this repo nightly, but nothing pulled it at the start of a session until this step existed, so a same-day handoff (worked on the Mac after lunch, picked up on Windows that evening) arrived with stale memory. Pull it before anything else reads it. If the pull brings in commits, say how many and name the newest, so it is visible that memory moved.

If any of the three has local uncommitted changes, commit them first with `<machine> snapshot before sync`, then pull, then push.

Merge note for `global-memory`: `transcripts/.errors.log` and `MEMORY.md` are both append-heavy and both machines write them. On conflict, keep both sides' content rather than choosing one — these are logs, not settings, and a dropped line is a lost memory.

## Step 2: inventory (always show before changing anything)

Walk `DEV/*`, `DEV/Football/*`, and `DEV/SpecialRequests/*`. Skip `.claude`, `_tools`, `_DRIVE` (a link to the Google Drive primary storage drive, not a project; never init it, never walk into it), `token-dashboard` (someone else's remote), and any folder ending in `_OLD_merged*`. For each folder report one of:

- **repo + erash11 remote**: uncommitted count, unpushed count
- **repo, no remote**: needs `gh repo create`
- **not a repo**: needs init + create (use the `new-project` skill's file set)

Then `gh repo list erash11 --limit 300 --json name` and list repos with no local folder. Skip: `dotclaude` (that is `~/.claude`), `SecondBrain`, `claude-skills`, `claude-memory-compiler`, `DEV`, `DexaProject`.

Eric pre-approves these operations; the inventory is for visibility, not a pause for approval, unless something looks wrong (a repo with hundreds of uncommitted files, a large file about to be added).

**Group the report by activity, not alphabetically.** Run `~/.claude/scripts/dev-activity.sh` (Mac) or `dev-activity.ps1` (Windows), which ranks repos by distinct commit days over 90 days. List the active ones individually and collapse the rest to a count: "118 dormant repos: all clean" is the useful line, not 118 names. About 14 repos are genuinely worked at any time; the rest are archives that happen to live in the same folder.

Rank by **commit days, not recency**. On 2026-09-09 a bulk migration gave 43 repos one commit each, after which every one of them looked active by any recency measure. Days-worked is not fooled by that, because a migration touches a repo once.

Nothing is archived or moved on the strength of this. Sorting is a reporting concern. Moving a dormant repo into an archive folder would break three things at once: `harvest-dev-docs` reads `<dir>/docs/*.md` without recursing, so archived repos would silently drop out of the memsearch index; KeystoneOS `projects.json`, `memory-sources.json`, `memory-index-paths.json` and `discovery-roots.json` hold DEV paths; and Tier A project memory is keyed by a slug derived from the absolute path, so moving a repo orphans its memory. Checked 2026-09-12. Do not revive the archive idea without fixing all three first.

## Step 3: apply, per repo

1. If uncommitted: put any untracked file over 95 MB and any `.env` into `.gitignore`, then `git add -A && git commit -m "<machine> snapshot before sync"`.
2. `git fetch origin` then `git merge --no-edit origin/<branch>`.
3. On conflict: keep this machine's version, save the remote version beside it as `<file>.from-mac` or `<file>.from-windows` (whichever the other machine is), stage both, commit. Never discard either side. `.DS_Store` conflicts: just delete the file.

   Save the remote side by **moving the file, never by redirecting stdout**. A
   redirect re-encodes the bytes; on Windows that silently mangles every
   non-ASCII character (an em-dash becomes `ΓÇö`) and adds a UTF-8 BOM, so the
   saved copy is corrupt and every later diff shows a phantom first-line change.

   - PowerShell: `git checkout --theirs -- <f>; Move-Item <f> <f>.from-mac; git checkout --ours -- <f>`
   - bash: `git checkout --theirs -- <f> && mv <f> <f>.from-mac && git checkout --ours -- <f>`

   Never run `git add -A` while `.git/MERGE_HEAD` exists — it stages the
   conflict markers themselves and commits a broken file. Stage only the named
   paths you just resolved.
4. `git push`.
5. Missing locally: `gh repo clone erash11/<name> DEV/<name>`.
6. No remote: `gh repo create erash11/<name> --private --source=. --push`.

Windows note: line-ending noise (`LF will be replaced by CRLF`) is normal. If a merge refuses to start because of phantom modifications, run `git add --renormalize .` and commit before merging.

Stale-lock note: if a commit or push fails with `cannot lock ref 'HEAD'`, check
`pgrep -fl git` (or `Get-Process git`) first. If no git is running and the
`.git/*.lock` file is zero bytes and older than the session, it is stale from an
interrupted run. Move it aside — do not delete it — then retry.

## Step 4: verify and report

Re-walk every repo. Report: DEV root used, config and skills pulled (yes/no), repos checked, pulled, cloned, created, and any folder still dirty or unpushed. List every `.from-*` file created so Eric can reconcile them. Finish with one line: clean or not.

## Step 5: pick up where the other machine left off

Syncing git state is only half the job. The other half is loading the context that came with it, and nothing else does this — the SessionStart hook injects global memory, but project state lives in the repo, and Tier A project memory does not cross machines because its slug is built from a path that differs per machine. This step is the only place that context gets read back in.

Do this for the repo Eric names, or the one he is in. If he has not named one, pick from the ACTIVE list in Step 2, not from all 132: take the active repo with the most recent commit and say which you chose. A dormant repo receiving one migration commit must never win this, which is exactly what picking by recency across everything would do.

1. Read `<repo>/AGENTS.md` (or `CLAUDE.md` if there is no AGENTS.md).
2. Read `<repo>/docs/STATUS.md`.
3. Read the newest file in `<repo>/docs/handoffs/`, if the folder exists and its newest file is within about two weeks.
4. If `docs/STATUS.md` does not exist in a repo that has real work in it, say so — that repo is invisible to the other machine and closeout should have created it.

Then report, in six lines or fewer, before doing any work:

```
Picking up: <repo>
Last session: <date>, <mac|windows>
Where things stand: <two lines from STATUS.md Current state>
Blocked on: <open questions, or "nothing">
Next: <top one or two from STATUS.md Next>
```

Stop there and wait for Eric to confirm or redirect. Do not start the next task off the back of STATUS.md on your own — it records where work stopped, not what he wants to do this morning.

## Do not

- Do not `rm` anything. Move to a `_to_delete` or `_OLD_*` folder if something must get out of the way.
- Do not rebase or force-push.
- Do not push DexaProject or any repo whose CLAUDE.md says its data must stay local.

#!/bin/bash
# Read-only DEV inventory: fetch each repo, print one TSV line per folder.
# status  name  branch  dirty  ahead  behind  remote
DEV=/Users/kristinarash/DEV
for d in "$DEV"/*/ "$DEV"/Football/*/ "$DEV"/SpecialRequests/*/; do
  d=${d%/}
  n=${d#$DEV/}
  base=$(basename "$d")
  case "$base" in
    .claude|_tools|_DRIVE|token-dashboard|*_OLD_merged*) continue ;;
  esac
  [ -L "$d" ] && continue
  if [ ! -e "$d/.git" ]; then
    # Group folders (Football, SpecialRequests) are containers, not projects
    case "$n" in Football|SpecialRequests) continue ;; esac
    printf 'NOREPO\t%s\n' "$n"; continue
  fi
  remote=$(git -C "$d" remote get-url origin 2>/dev/null)
  br=$(git -C "$d" branch --show-current 2>/dev/null)
  dirty=$(git -C "$d" status --porcelain 2>/dev/null | wc -l | tr -d ' ')
  if [ -z "$remote" ]; then
    printf 'NOREMOTE\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$n" "$br" "$dirty"; continue
  fi
  git -C "$d" fetch --quiet origin 2>/dev/null || { printf 'FETCHFAIL\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$n" "$br" "$dirty" "$remote"; continue; }
  if git -C "$d" rev-parse --verify --quiet "origin/$br" >/dev/null; then
    counts=$(git -C "$d" rev-list --left-right --count "HEAD...origin/$br" 2>/dev/null)
    ahead=${counts%%[[:space:]]*}; behind=${counts##*[[:space:]]}
  else
    ahead=NOUPSTREAM; behind=0
  fi
  printf 'REPO\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$n" "$br" "$dirty" "$ahead" "$behind" "$remote"
done

## Next actions, most important first
1. Rotate the exposed VALD client secret. Still live in private Git history.
2. Re-file `agent-skills/_recovered-from-codex/` into real skill folders, then delete it.
3. Delete `~/Documents/Codex` when ready. Marked, not deleted, at Eric's request.

## Mid-flight
Nothing. Everything committed and pushed.

## Addendum: re-filing the recovered scripts (same day)

`agent-skills/_recovered-from-codex/` was emptied and retired. Two of its five scripts
turned out to be byte-identical (SHA256) to files already tracked in dotclaude at
`skills-archive/2026-07-24-os-audit/gsap/scripts/extract-audio-data.py` and
`.../remotion-to-hyperframes/scripts/lint_source.py`. They were dropped, not duplicated.

The three genuinely unique ones landed here:
- `ZoteroInjestion/scripts/prepare_publication_syntheses.py` (e09892a) — it hardcodes
  paths to the zotero-research-bridge db and SportScienceResearchRepo
- `CLI_Dev/codex-win-to-mac-migration/project_migration.py` + `tests/` + README (cdb1bcd)
- Holding folder moved to `_to_delete/2026-09-14_recovered-from-codex/` (4cf5670)

### The real lesson from today
Three times this session a file was reported missing or unique based on a recursive
PowerShell filename scan, and all three were wrong. `Get-ChildItem -Recurse` silently
skips paths past the Windows 260-character limit, and the remotion test-corpus tree
blows through it. Errors are swallowed even without `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue`
showing anything useful.

Rules going forward:
- Inside a repo, use `git ls-files` to ask whether a file exists. It reads the index and
  does not care about path length.
- Never claim two files are duplicates by name. Compare SHA256.
- Never claim a file is unique from one scan. Confirm with a second method.

# Closeout

One command that replaces the manual end-of-day sequence: "any loose ends?" → "commit and push what needs to be" → "is this in memory?" → "write a handoff so Codex can pick this up."

Run all five checks, then give ONE verdict. Do not ask permission between steps — the invocation of this skill IS the authorization for the full sequence. Commit and push is standing-authorized for every DEV repo: each repo's `AGENTS.md` Session routine says "update STATUS, commit, push at end", and unpushed work on one machine is the top cause of conflicts on the other. The only exceptions are repos whose `CLAUDE.md` says their data must stay local (DexaProject is the precedent); commit those locally and list them as open.

## Step 1 — Loose-ends sweep

- `git status` across **every** repo in DEV, not only the ones named in this conversation. Another session, another harness, or the other machine may have left work dirty, and a closeout that only checks what it remembers touching will say "clear to sign off" over someone else's uncommitted work. Walk `DEV/`, `DEV/Football/` and `DEV/SpecialRequests/`, and report any repo with uncommitted or unpushed commits. The full walk takes about 90 seconds.
  - Windows: `git -C <repo> status --porcelain` per repo. Do NOT use `Get-ChildItem -Recurse` to look for files; it silently skips paths past the 260-character limit. Inside a repo, `git ls-files` is the reliable way to ask whether a file exists.
  - Repos with dirty state you did not touch: commit and push them like any other, and name them in the report so the user knows another session left them.
- Unfinished todos/tasks from this session (TaskList if available).
